# Explore the AI & ML curriculum

**6 guided foundation days · 41 modules · 205 further learning sessions**

Browse what you will practice before downloading the app. This index is generated from the same curriculum used by First Principles; it lists every module, session title, prerequisite, observable outcome, and module project.

**[Download edition 03](https://github.com/MJmuhammadjihad/AI-ML-Engineering-Roadmap/releases/download/v3.0.1/first-principles-atlas-v3.html)** · [Project introduction](../README.md) · [How the curriculum is maintained](../CONTRIBUTING.md)

## Where to begin

If you are starting from zero, open the app and choose **Today → Start this lesson**. The six guided foundation days take a Python study-budget calculator from a saved file to a validated command-line tool. After the foundations, use **Path** to explore a career route and its prerequisites.

A day is a study budget, not a deadline. The default foundation plan allocates 360 active minutes with 90 break minutes additional; you can spread the work across more calendar days. Neither six foundation days nor completing the atlas guarantees job readiness.

The eight sections below group related subjects. They are **not one fixed execution order**: prerequisites cross section boundaries. Follow the linked prerequisite modules and the app’s selected route. Each module also includes practice, checks, a worked example, and a transfer task in the app.

## Jump to a subject

<a id="guided-foundation-days"></a>
## Guided foundation days

<a id="foundation-01"></a>
### Day 01 · Make a saved file do useful arithmetic

**What you will demonstrate:** Save, run, test, and explain a Python study-budget calculator that distinguishes active study from elapsed time.

**Planning budget:** 360 active minutes + 90 break minutes. These are estimates; carry unfinished work forward.

<a id="foundation-02"></a>
### Day 02 · Turn typed text into measured quantities

**What you will demonstrate:** Build an interactive minute-budget calculator and express totals as whole hours plus remaining minutes.

**Planning budget:** 360 active minutes + 90 break minutes. These are estimates; carry unfinished work forward.

<a id="foundation-03"></a>
### Day 03 · Make decisions and reject impossible ranges

**What you will demonstrate:** Validate integer time ranges, enforce a chosen 24-hour planning window, and print one correct target classification.

**Planning budget:** 360 active minutes + 90 break minutes. These are estimates; carry unfinished work forward.

<a id="foundation-04"></a>
### Day 04 · Repeat useful work without copying it

**What you will demonstrate:** Collect repeated study blocks, maintain a running total, and explain every iteration with a trace table.

**Planning budget:** 360 active minutes + 90 break minutes. These are estimates; carry unfinished work forward.

<a id="foundation-05"></a>
### Day 05 · Give a calculation a clear contract

**What you will demonstrate:** Define, call, test, and explain small functions that return calculated values without collecting input or printing inside them.

**Planning budget:** 360 active minutes + 90 break minutes. These are estimates; carry unfinished work forward.

<a id="foundation-06"></a>
### Day 06 · Deliver a small program with an honest test record

**What you will demonstrate:** Build a three-block planning tool that handles malformed numeric text, validates its constraints, and explains planned, available, and unassigned study time.

**Planning budget:** 360 active minutes + 90 break minutes. These are estimates; carry unfinished work forward.

<a id="phase-foundations"></a>
## Foundations

<a id="c01"></a>
### C01 · Think in problems, evidence, and algorithms

Learn to turn an ambiguous wish into a small, testable computational problem before choosing a model.

**Prerequisites:** No prior core module. Beginners should start with the guided foundation days.

<details>
<summary>View the five sessions, outcomes, and project</summary>

**Learning sessions**

1. Define the decision before the solution
2. Represent the world with explicit data
3. Decompose a process into small algorithms
4. Estimate effort and search systematically
5. Build a paper baseline and falsify it

**What you will demonstrate**

- Write measurable acceptance criteria
- Trace a simple algorithm by hand
- Separate observed facts from assumptions

**Module project:** The support-ticket decision brief

</details>

<a id="c02"></a>

2. Make decisions with conditions
3. Repeat work without losing control
4. Use errors as diagnostic evidence
5. Ship your first small terminal program

</details>

<summary>View the five sessions, outcomes, and project</summary>

**Learning sessions**

1. Choose collections by their behavior
2. Design functions as small contracts

<a id="c04"></a>

Make small programs recoverable, testable, reviewable, and reproducible on another machine.

<a id="b01"></a>
### B01 · Algorithms: choose the work before optimizing it

Build a tiny document index while learning invariants, search, complexity, graphs, and honest measurement.

**Prerequisites:** [C03 · Functions, collections, and structured data](#c03)

<details>
<summary>View the five sessions, outcomes, and project</summary>

**Learning sessions**

**What you will demonstrate**

## Machine learning

<a id="c12"></a>
### C12 · Formulate machine learning and prevent leakage

Translate a real decision into a learning problem, choose honest splits, and establish baselines before model complexity.

**Prerequisites:** [C11 · Explore data without fooling yourself](#c11), [C08 · Linear algebra as geometry and computation](#c08), [C09 · Probability as reasoning under uncertainty](#c09)

<summary>View the five sessions, outcomes, and project</summary>

**Learning sessions**

5. Seal the evaluation design before tuning

**What you will demonstrate**

- Define features, targets, prediction time, and decision policy

**Module project:** A leak-resistant prediction charter

<a id="phase-ai-systems"></a>
## AI systems

<a id="c22"></a>
### C22 · Retrieval and grounded generation

Build a retrieval system that can find useful evidence, respect access boundaries, and support answers that are easy to inspect.

**Prerequisites:** [C17 · Unsupervised structure and nearest-neighbor retrieval](#c17), [C21 · Language models from tokens to transformers](#c21)

<details>
<summary>View the five sessions, outcomes, and project</summary>

**Learning sessions**

1. Search quality begins with a query and relevant evidence

**What you will demonstrate**

- Compare lexical and dense retrieval on labeled queries

<a id="c23"></a>
### C23 · Evaluate language-model behavior and tool use

**What you will demonstrate**

<a id="c24"></a>

**Learning sessions**

**What you will demonstrate**

<a id="b04"></a>
### B04 · Adapt a model without weakening the evidence

Choose between prompting, retrieval and parameter updates; build a controlled small adaptation experiment before spending substantial compute.

**Prerequisites:** [C19 · PyTorch: reliable training as an engineering loop](#c19), [C21 · Language models from tokens to transformers](#c21), [C23 · Evaluate language-model behavior and tool use](#c23)

<details>
<summary>View the five sessions, outcomes, and project</summary>

**Learning sessions**

<a id="a05"></a>
### A05 · Serving models within latency and memory budgets

Measure the full inference path, choose a serving strategy, and improve throughput without hiding quality or reliability costs.

**Prerequisites:** [A04 · Reproducible packages, containers, and CI](#a04), [C19 · PyTorch: reliable training as an engineering loop](#c19)

<details>
<summary>View the five sessions, outcomes, and project</summary>

**Learning sessions**

1. Locate time in the complete inference path
2. Reason about arrivals, queues, and overload
3. Trade batch efficiency against waiting time
4. Optimize one bottleneck and verify the cost
5. Distinguish liveness, readiness, and useful behavior

**What you will demonstrate**

- Measure end-to-end and component latency distributions.
- Explain batching, concurrency, queueing, and memory tradeoffs.
- Validate a serving optimization against both quality and performance criteria.

**Module project:** Measured inference service

</details>

<a id="a06"></a>
### A06 · Cloud architecture, identity, and secure operations

Map a small ML service onto cloud primitives while controlling permissions, secrets, network exposure, and spending.

**Prerequisites:** [A02 · APIs, backends, and durable data contracts](#a02), [A04 · Reproducible packages, containers, and CI](#a04)

<details>
<summary>View the five sessions, outcomes, and project</summary>

**Learning sessions**

1. Translate a workload into cloud primitives
2. Grant actions to identities, not machines by habit
3. Keep secrets out of distribution paths
4. Minimize exposure and bound spending
5. Rehearse deployment without overstating evidence

**What you will demonstrate**

- Explain compute, object storage, database, and network boundaries.
- Apply least-privilege identities and secret separation.
- Document deployment and cost controls without requiring a paid account.

**Module project:** Least-privilege deployment blueprint

</details>

<a id="a07"></a>
### A07 · Data pipelines that preserve meaning over time

Build a repeatable data pipeline with contracts, temporal correctness, lineage, and explicit recovery behavior.

**Prerequisites:** [C06 · Data modeling and SQL](#c06), [C16 · Feature pipelines and reproducible data boundaries](#c16)

<details>
<summary>View the five sessions, outcomes, and project</summary>

**Learning sessions**

1. Define stages, ownership, and contracts
2. Make reruns and partial failures recoverable
3. Respect event time and information availability
4. Backfill with explicit scope and quality gates
5. Orchestrate dependencies and trace lineage

**What you will demonstrate**

- Model batch stages and their data contracts.
- Handle time, duplicates, and backfills without leaking future information.
- Trace a model input to its source and pipeline version.

**Module project:** Versioned feature pipeline

</details>

<a id="a08"></a>
### A08 · Monitoring, drift, and incident response

Observe whether an ML service remains available, useful, and safe after release, and practice responding when it does not.

**Prerequisites:** [A05 · Serving models within latency and memory budgets](#a05), [C15 · Evaluation: decisions, uncertainty, and calibration](#c15)

<details>
<summary>View the five sessions, outcomes, and project</summary>

**Learning sessions**

1. Define the behavior that must remain healthy
2. Instrument with enough context and minimal exposure
3. Distinguish data shift from quality degradation
4. Create alerts that lead to decisions
5. Rehearse an incident and learn from recovery

**What you will demonstrate**

- Separate service health, data quality, and model quality metrics.
- Interpret drift with delayed labels and operational context.
- Write actionable alerts and rehearse incident response.

**Module project:** ML service operations dossier

</details>

<a id="a09"></a>
### A09 · Designing ML systems under real constraints

Turn a prediction objective into a defensible system design, balancing data freshness, reliability, experimentation, latency, and cost.

**Prerequisites:** [A07 · Data pipelines that preserve meaning over time](#a07), [A08 · Monitoring, drift, and incident response](#a08)

<details>
<summary>View the five sessions, outcomes, and project</summary>

**Learning sessions**

1. Start with the decision and the service contract
2. Choose batch, online, or hybrid execution
3. Estimate capacity and measure tail behavior
4. Evaluate a change with a controlled experiment
5. Calculate unit economics and document tradeoffs

**What you will demonstrate**

- Translate a user decision into data, quality, reliability, and cost requirements.
- Compare batch, online, and hybrid designs using stated assumptions.
- Design safe experiments and calculate workload-dependent unit economics.

**Module project:** A decision-centered ML system design

</details>

<a id="a10"></a>
### A10 · Responsible AI, privacy, and security boundaries

Analyze how an ML system can harm users, disclose data, or exceed its authority, then turn those concerns into testable controls.

**Prerequisites:** [C15 · Evaluation: decisions, uncertainty, and calibration](#c15)

<details>
<summary>View the five sessions, outcomes, and project</summary>

**Learning sessions**

1. Map stakeholders and plausible harms
2. Evaluate slices and competing fairness objectives
3. Minimize data and define its lifecycle
4. Place authorization outside the model
5. Publish limits and rehearse escalation

**What you will demonstrate**

- Map stakeholders, data flows, and harmful failure scenarios.
- Evaluate relevant performance slices without treating one fairness metric as universally sufficient.
- Apply least privilege and test boundaries around sensitive data and untrusted model inputs.

**Module project:** A tested risk and control dossier

</details>

<a id="b02"></a>
### B02 · Computers, processes, and networks beneath the API

Trace bytes from a file through a process and an HTTP request, then build a bounded local service experiment.

**Prerequisites:** [C04 · Engineering habits: Git, tests, and reproducibility](#c04)

<details>
<summary>View the five sessions, outcomes, and project</summary>

**Learning sessions**

1. Represent information as bytes with a contract
2. Separate running memory from durable state
3. Control a worker as an operating-system process
4. Trace a request through distinct protocol layers
5. Bound resources before increasing concurrency

**What you will demonstrate**

- Distinguish characters, encoded bytes, memory, files and persistent state
- Explain processes, exit codes, streams, timeouts and resource limits
- Trace a request through DNS, transport, TLS and HTTP without treating them as one layer

**Module project:** A bounded local worker and request trace

</details>

<a id="phase-career-research"></a>
## Career &amp; research

<a id="a11"></a>
### A11 · Research replication and mathematical depth

Read a technical claim as an argument, reconstruct its mathematics and experiment, and reproduce a bounded result before attempting an extension.

**Prerequisites:** [C19 · PyTorch: reliable training as an engineering loop](#c19), [C21 · Language models from tokens to transformers](#c21), [B05 · Mathematical depth for research](#b05)

<details>
<summary>View the five sessions, outcomes, and project</summary>

**Learning sessions**

1. Read a paper as a structured argument
2. Connect equations to tensor operations
3. Build a reproducible experiment before scaling
4. Design one ablation that can answer a question
5. Explain discrepancies and communicate limits

**What you will demonstrate**

- Translate a paper into a claim, assumptions, algorithm, and evaluation protocol.
- Derive a relevant gradient and check it numerically.
- Run controlled replications and report discrepancies, uncertainty, and negative results.

**Module project:** A small, honest replication study

</details>

<a id="a12"></a>
### A12 · Portfolio evidence and a global job-search practice

Translate demonstrated ability into a clear portfolio, evaluate current job requirements systematically, and practice communicating technical decisions.

**Prerequisites:** [C15 · Evaluation: decisions, uncertainty, and calibration](#c15)

<details>
<summary>View the five sessions, outcomes, and project</summary>

**Learning sessions**

1. Sample the market as data, not as a slogan
2. Build an evidence map for one target role
3. Write a case study that survives inspection
4. Practice interviews as observable reasoning
5. Run an ethical application and improvement loop

**What you will demonstrate**

- Analyze a dated sample of relevant job postings without claiming it represents the entire global market.
- Package a role-specific capstone with reproducible evidence and honest limitations.
- Practice technical explanations, problem solving, applications, and feedback-driven iteration.

**Module project:** An evidence-backed career dossier

</details>

<a id="b05"></a>
### B05 · Mathematical depth for research

Translate derivatives, constraints, estimators and information objectives into small experiments whose assumptions and conclusions can be inspected.

**Prerequisites:** [C08 · Linear algebra as geometry and computation](#c08), [C09 · Probability as reasoning under uncertainty](#c09), [C10 · Statistics, experiments, and causal restraint](#c10), [C19 · PyTorch: reliable training as an engineering loop](#c19)

<details>
<summary>View the five sessions, outcomes, and project</summary>

**Learning sessions**

1. Derive a vector gradient and test its direction
2. Separate constraints from poor conditioning
3. Study estimators as repeated procedures
4. Connect information objectives to probability assumptions
5. Design a mathematical claim that code can challenge

**What you will demonstrate**

- Derive vector gradients with explicit shapes and check them through directional perturbations
- Distinguish constraints, curvature, conditioning and numerical precision in optimization behavior
- Explain estimator bias, variance and uncertainty without treating a finite simulation as proof
- Connect cross-entropy and KL divergence to an explicit probability model and support assumptions
- Produce a reproducible mathematical experiment with baselines, falsifiable predictions and bounded conclusions

**Module project:** A derivation-to-experiment research notebook

</details>

## Source and scope

Generated from [`src/data.json`](../src/data.json) and [`src/foundations.json`](../src/foundations.json). Curriculum revision: **2026-11-05**. Module IDs are stable links; the full explanations, exercises, worked examples, and assessment rubrics live in the app.

Module outcomes describe what to practice and demonstrate, not a certification. Study durations are authored planning budgets. See [the validation record](../VALIDATION.md) for executed checks and [the market research](../research/v3-market-research.md) for source dates and sampling limits.

To correct a title, prerequisite, or outcome, [suggest a lesson improvement](https://github.com/MJmuhammadjihad/AI-ML-Engineering-Roadmap/issues/new?template=lesson_improvement.yml) and include its module ID. To edit the curriculum, change the source JSON and run `python3 scripts/build_curriculum.py`.
